#44887. Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3250 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters.
  • Some significant bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land.
  • But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters. A whitetail lives the 3½ years necessary to grow a bragging set of antlers by learning to cope with the annual influx of hunters during the season’s first days. Every opening day that the buck survives increases his chance of surviving the ensuing openers, as well.

Some significant bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land. Others crawl into the most inaccessible and gosh-awful cover their “territory” has to offer — the kind of place hunters walk around, rather than through — and stay there until the crowds leave. And on more than one occasion, I have found a bruiser buck in a tiny, secluded patch of isolated cover — the kind of place most hunters never think to look in.

But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf. You can bet that once the steady crack of opening day rifles slackens to only an occasional pop, those big bucks will be right back to business as usual. And that is the precise reason why your best chance for bagging a wall-hanger occurs after the opening day madness has subsided.

In a recent development, where you begin your search for that after-the-opener buck hinges upon one factor: the rut. Many states initiative their firearms seasons to coincide with the rut, offering their hunters every opportunity to harvest the surplus bucks. Other states, bound in tradition, open the season after the main rut has ended. If you are planning to travel out of your home state to hunt whitetails, it makes sense to hunt a state where the season coincides with the rut, all other criteria being equal.

According to recent reports, A mature whitetail buck is a different character during the rut than he is after it. A buck’s sole purpose at that time is to procreate, and this he does with obvious enthusiasm and the stamina of a teenager. There are stories abounding in every deer camp in the country of the crazy antics performed by bucks under the spell of the “rutting moon,” such as lovesick bucks strolling across open fields in broad daylight. Others tell tales of bucks putting their noses to does’ tracks and following those tracks, even after being shot at and missed several times. Rut-crazed bucks, while under the influence of a powerful rush of hormones, have even been known to either pick fights with or attempt to mate with assorted farm livestock.

It has been revealed that so rampant are the stories that I’m afraid there exists a whole contingent of deer hunters laboring under the false assumption that all a hunter needs do to down one of these crazy buggers is to walk into the woods, lean up against a stump and wait for one of the poor, sex-addled dummies to saunter on by. Although such tactics work just often enough to keep the myth perpetuated, plenty of hunters have been sitting against stumps for more unsuccessful years than they will probably admit, and they’re still waiting for a buck to wander by.

Hunting whitetails during the rut and after the opening weekend of the season isn’t easy. You must employ all of the skill and woods savvy you have. Any breaks you receive because of a buck’s overactive glands should be considered a bonus.

According to recent reports, after the opener, I refine my hunting strategy for major bucks by determining what stage the rut is in. This is vital because the stage of the rut will determine where I concentrate most of my midweek hunting efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the whitetail buck is ready to breed long before the first doe enters estrus. During this period, the buck runs off excess energy by beating up saplings, sparring with bushes and, on occasion, duking it out with other bucks. In the process of making rubs on bushes and trees, the buck deposits scents that tell the rest of the whitetail community who was there.

It has been revealed that scrapes begin to show up in increasing numbers as the level of testosterone builds in the buck’s system. The buck paws out scrapes and leaves his scent both in the bare earth of the scrapes and on overhanging branches above the scrapes. Again, this is a means of communicating with other whitetails. The message to does is that the buck is now standing at stud, and it tells other bucks that they had best move along if they know what’s good for them.

A buck will paw out most of his scrapes in areas where they are most likely to be seen or smelled by does. Openings in woods, old logging roads and the edges of woodlots are common places to encounter scrapes. A buck may make a dozen or more scrapes, and he’ll check some of them daily, making sure they are free of debris and liberally doused with musk/urine. These are the scrapes to hunt over.

Recent findings suggest that however, once the does begin cycling into heat, the dominant bucks that handle the bulk of the breeding chores are often so busy accompanying, tracking and servicing does that they neither have the time nor the need to freshen their scrapes. But if you find a string of scrapes that have not been freshened for several days, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the rut is over or that the buck that made the scrapes is hanging from someone else’s game pole. It may mean that the buck is out doing his job.

The best way to determine what stage the rut is in is to spend a day or two in the woods prior to the hunt. If fresh scrapes abound, you will be hunting the pre-coital period, and a stand near a scrape line is going to be hard to beat. If, on the other hand, you find that more than half of the scrapes are old and abandoned, it’s a good bet that the massive bucks are out taking care of the does, while the lesser bucks are still hanging around their scrapes, waiting.

If you just don’t have time to get into the woods prior to the season, you can get a good idea about the stage of the rut by speaking with area game managers, milk haulers, rural school bus drivers, postal carriers, loggers, trappers, farmers, grouse hunters, bowhunters or others who spend most of their time in deer country. If the bucks are chasing the does, chances are these people will have observed some of the activity.

According to recent reports, why all of the fuss over determining what stage the rut is in? Because it makes a big difference when you have to decide how you want to hunt after the opening weekend of the season.

Sources indicate that when the season begins, if the actual breeding season has not yet begun but bucks are busy pawing out upcoming scrapes and freshening old ones, chances are the bucks will curtail this activity during the high-pressure days at the beginning of the season, resuming their rounds once the hunters thin out. I like to have at least a half-dozen scrape lines pinpointed prior to the opener, and I check them after the opening weekend for any sign of activity. I then concentrate my hunting efforts near the “hottest” scrapes.

Recent findings suggest that if your pre-season scouting and snooping indicates that the actual breeding season is in progress, then hunting over scrapes may not be your best option for tagging a really good buck. Remember, it is often the significant, dominant bucks in the area that handle the bulk of the breeding chores. Even in an area with an excellent buck-to-doe ratio, a breeding buck can be kept so busy that he has little time or need to tend his scrapes. Often, a buck will spend 24 hours with the same doe, breeding her several times before her cycle ends. At this time, it is the doe, not the buck, that determines where the pair will travel. Though I would not totally rule out hunting in the vicinity of inactive scrapes at this stage of the rut, there are other options that I’ve found give me a better chance at tagging a big buck.

One of my favorite methods during this period is to concentrate my hunting efforts in areas where I have encountered good numbers of does in the past. Does and fawns tend to hang around together, and they routinely congregate in specific areas, often bedding as a loosely knit group in a favorite swale or sunny hillside. I can’t direct you to these “ladies-only bedrooms,” but I’ll bet there is such a place in the chunk of woods you hunt.

Sources indicate that you can locate these places that hold special favor with the does by simply noting those areas where you encounter the most doe activity. After a few years of hunting the same ground, a familiar pattern becomes apparent.

According to recent reports, on several occasions, I have located a hotbed of doe activity by simply listening to other hunters. When you hear a hunter complain that he sat on his stand and saw 15 does but not a single buck, find out where he was sitting. You can bet that when the time is right, there will be a buck or two sniffing around the vicinity.

It has been revealed that A dominant buck ranges well out of his home area during the actual breeding season. I don’t think he goes out of his way looking for does so much as he is drawn out of the territory when following the tracks of a doe that has visited his scrapes or just wandered through the area. A buck engaged in this activity moves with a single-minded purpose, shuffling along, nose to the ground, seldom looking up, intent upon finding the maker of the tracks he is following. I once missed a buck that trailed a doe past my tree stand in this manner, my arrow slicing harmlessly over the buck’s back only to skitter noisily through the carpet of dry oak leaves a few yards beyond. The buck lifted his head and looked in the direction of the commotion. Apparently satisfied that whatever had made the racket was not what he was looking for, he then ambled on his way while I frantically fumbled around trying to nock another arrow.

When a buck finally tracks down a doe, as often as not, she will then lead the buck on a little chase that, in all likelihood, will take the buck still farther from his home base. By the time the buck actually mates with the doe, he may be miles from his original starting point. On the way back to his core area, it is not unlikely that the buck will cut the track of another “hot” doe and repeat the scenario.

All of this rambling makes it impossible to pattern a buck during the height of the breeding season, prompting many knowledgeable whitetail hunters to claim that taking a good buck during the peak of the rut is mostly a matter of luck. I disagree.

In a recent development, hunting near a known “doe hangout” can help. And you can stack the deck in your favor even more by hunting a funnel area near a concentration of does. A funnel is simply any natural or man-made feature of the terrain that restricts the movement of deer. An hourglass-shaped section of woods is the classic funnel. Deer moving from one wide portion of the hourglass to the other must pass through the narrow waist. In farm country, the funnel may be a brushy fenceline connecting two woodlots. In the rugged country of the West, where whitetails are becoming increasingly common, a jutting jaw of sheer rimrock can force whitetails into a confined passage. Funnels work well because even though a buck with a snootful of “hot” doe scent wouldn’t care if he was standing in the middle of Madison Avenue, the does do not lose their heads. Does will stick to cover when on the move, even when there is a grunting, panting Romeo dogging their every move.

Industry observers note that in many whitetail states, hunters are left with no choice but to hunt well after the main rutting period is over. At first, hunting after the opening weekend under these circumstances appears to be a futile endeavor. Without the promise of the rut to keep the bucks on the move, and with the absence of hunters to jar deer loose, what chance does the midweek hunter have of scoring on a decent buck? He has a pretty good one, I would say.

First, although the bulk of the breeding chores are completed in about a two-week period, there is still some activity after the main rut is over. Does that were not impregnated will cycle back into heat 28 days after their first estrus cycle ends. In some states, this is just about the time the rifle season rolls around. In addition, in some of the best whitetail areas, it is not uncommon for female fawns of the year to breed. This often applies to as many as 40 percent of them. Frequently, these young breeders experience their first estrus cycle later than older does. So, don’t strike out the possibility of the rut working in your favor even though the peak has passed. In that part of Minnesota where I live, the bulk of the breeding is completed by mid-November, yet each year, I find active scrapes late into November and even December. Last season, during an especially mild December, I found a pair of bushel-basket-size recently freshened scrapes while hunting grouse on New Year’s Eve day. If you can find these “late scrapes,” concentrate your hunting efforts near them.

But even if you fail to find any of these scrapes later in the year, you still stand a good chance of tagging a buck during the middle of the week if you let the after-effects of the rut work in your favor. During the rut, a buck takes little time out to eat. By the end of the breeding season, a buck that began the rut in peak condition can be drawn and thin, actually haggard looking. Some bucks lose up to 20 percent of their body weight during the course of the rut. Across the Northern states and Canada, where winter-kill is an annual problem, the major, breeding bucks follow the fawns in death each winter simply because they run off all of their reserve fat during the rut and are often unable to replenish it before the onset of winter snows.

In a recent development, although the largest bucks are often nocturnal in their feeding habits at other times of the year, when the rut is over, dominant bucks cannot afford to limit their foraging to the hours of darkness alone. In order to regain their strength and put on the layer of fat necessary to see them through the winter, they must forage during the day. This gives the after-the-opener hunter the chance he needs to find bucks up and about during shooting hours.

This need to feed heavily does not necessarily mean that a big buck will be found sauntering around an alfalfa field at high noon, scarfing down the last frost-tinged greens of the year. It does mean that rather than tucking himself safely away in a thicket long before the morning sun ever peeks over the ridge, a buck will now tend to linger at the feeding grounds longer in the morning. Does and fawns often feed for an hour after sunrise, and now, bucks will begin to do the same. In the evening, when they normally would not begin feeding until complete darkness had fallen, bucks will now arrive at the feeding sites earlier — often in that last precious minute of shooting light.

In a recent development, even at midday, the massive boys will not be content to simply lay in their beds and chew their cuds. I have noticed that once the rut is over, bucks are much more likely to rise from their beds and spend an hour or two at midday — often between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. — browsing near their bedding sites.

All of this daylight activity is a massive plus for the after-the-opener hunter who must depend upon natural deer movements, rather than other hunters, to put a buck in front of him. The natural inclination is to hunt from a stand near the feeding area, but this is a mistake when you’re after mature bucks. A big buck is constantly alert, using each of his senses to detect the slightest hint of danger. Never is a buck more alert than when he is feeding during shooting light because he knows he is most vulnerable then. The bucks I have observed feeding during the season have been wound-up tighter than a watch spring and ready to snap at the slightest provocation. One miscue on your part, whether it is movement or scent or whatever, will send him running. I try to avoid known feeding areas, and I concentrate my efforts near the bedding areas.

It has been revealed that hunting near the bedding area means that any shot I take will most often be attempted in good light. That’s vital for a clean kill. A buck may not arrive back at his bedding area until the sun is an hour high in the morning, and he may leave his bed to begin a dawdling trip to the feeding area in late afternoon. Instead of risking a poor shot at a shadowy form in the gray gloom of dusk or dawn, I take my shot when the light is in my favor.

Industry observers note that also, by concentrating my efforts in the vicinity of the buck’s daytime haunts, I have a better chance of catching him up and about during the midday hours. If I am forced to move into the bedding area and take a stand at mid-morning, I risk detection by the buck. But if I move into my stand in the dark and set up quietly, I double my chances of scoring. If I fail to take the buck as he returns from breakfast, I will be there waiting when he gets up for lunch or dinner.

But you don’t have to confine yourself to a stand. If conditions allow for quiet stillhunting, I like nothing better than to either prowl the edges of a buck’s daytime haunts or simply tread my way along a ridge littered with the acorns of the white oak, moving only a few yards at a time and stopping often to look, listen and feel. Often after the crowds of opening day are gone from the woods for another year, it is just me and the deer — one-on-one. And that’s the way I like it best.

#44885. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1543 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no intends for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no intends for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

Recent findings suggest that on the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

In a recent development, we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

It has been revealed that linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden remarked, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

According to recent reports, linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Recent findings suggest that survival swiftly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

In a recent development, one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling blueprint was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden mentioned. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other prepares. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

It has been revealed that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden noted. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

According to recent reports, pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden stated, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

According to recent reports, when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Sources indicate that her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

It has been revealed that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden remarked. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

It has been revealed that overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine. We flag what you give up at each price, so beginners and casual skiers can shop smart. Skiers facing harsh weather may still want premium shells and insulation. Costco’s stock changes fast, so grab what you want early.

According to recent reports, with groceries and gas so pricey, it’s no wonder so many of us are turning to Costco. Everyone knows the warehouse is a deal machine for electronics, home goods, and tires, but this time of year, the aisles are also stocked with a surprising array of ski gear at steep discounts.

According to recent reports, plenty of skiers assume outdoor gear from substantial-box stores and other non-specialty retailers can’t be trusted. At Costco, that’s not necessarily true. The warehouse pulls in items from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, and Head, and its seasoned members know a steal when they see one. A Spyder full-zip sweater jacket for $30 or less? That goes straight in the cart. Buy now, try on at home: Costco’s “satisfaction guaranteed” return policy means you can easily take back whatever doesn’t work out.

Sources indicate that the catch: buying ski gear from a warehouse means making compromises. A specialty ski shop has gear with premium features like name-brand insulation and weatherproof materials (and premium prices to match). If you’re outside for hours in gnarly weather, you may need those technical features to stay warm and dry. But casual skiers, beginners, and kids will find plenty of choices at Costco, and experts can find some gems, too. It’s the perfect place for a comfy fleece, a reasonably priced heated vest, a MIPS helmet, affordable gloves and goggles, and après-ski accessories. SKI recommends the following items, but act fast because, like a powder day, the goods won’t last.

Fine print: you’ll need a Costco membership to snag any of these, so factor the annual fee into your budget.

Smith is a specialty-shop staple, so finding the Survey on the Costco website is a legit surprise. This all-mountain lid pairs MIPS with Koroyd zones that keep the weight down. An integrated ChromaPop visor stands in for goggles and works with glasses, and a dial fine-tunes the fit.

It has been revealed that compromise: There really isn’t one. You get a top-shelf helmet at Costco pricing (it retails for around $260 elsewhere). If you weren’t a visor-helmet person before now, maybe you just became one?

This is the budget way to get a MIPS-equipped helmet on your head, and it hits the feature checklist. Three-stage vents let you dump heat on sunny laps, the earpads come out when spring arrives, and a built-in goggle lock keeps most goggles from sliding off the back. An adjustable retention system helps dial in the fit, and it comes in four sizes, small through extra large.

Compromise: You get the safety and venting, but not the luxe features of a premium helmet, like a plush lining or a magnetic chin buckle.

Magnetic lens swap systems are usually a perk of pricier goggles, but Nordik includes one in these affordable goggles. The HOD’s magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out in seconds, and the box includes a second, low-light lens so you’re covered when the sun disappears. The oversized spherical lens has anti-fog treatment and UV400 protection, and the roomy OTG frame fits over large glasses and runs medium to large. A carrying case is thrown in, too.

Compromise: You’re not getting top-of-the-line lenses with light-adapting tech, so you’ll swap lenses by hand when conditions change.

It has been revealed that when it comes to ski mittens, leather is king, and getting a deerskin outer at Costco prices is a serious bargain. Deerskin naturally sheds water and wind and holds up to season after season of abuse, the kind of toughness synthetic shells struggle to match. These pair that shell with 150-gram 3M Thinsulate and a waterproof, breathable insert. The extended gauntlet cuff, with an adjustable strap and cinch cord, seals out powder.

Compromise: You’re not getting a branded waterproof membrane like Gore-Tex, so don’t count on premium storm performance.

Industry observers note that you can outfit the entire family with Head’s ski gloves thanks to a size run ranging from XS to XL. With a combination of lightweight and breathable insulation and a waterproof/windproof insert, the gloves keep hands warm on milder ski days, with an exterior zippered pocket for handwarmers. Touchscreen technology means you can access your smartphone without removing your gloves.

Sources indicate that compromise: If you spend less than $25 on gloves, don’t expect them to hold up to prolonged exposure to super cold temps or wet weather. (You’d have to spend at least $100 more for that.) Durability may be a weakness too, as the soft polyester material on the palm could peel off with use.

Recent findings suggest that dakine, born in Hawaii in 1979 and now a fixture in ski and snowboard shops, is another name you won’t expect to find next to the paper towels. This insulated midweight jacket has the details kids actually use: an inner powder skirt, a storm shield inside the hood, and two zippered side pockets. The hood comes off when it’s not needed, and sizes run XS–XL for the growth spurts that make buying premium kids’ gear hurt.

Industry observers note that pair it with the snow pants for a budget head-to-toe outfit. The insulated pants are wind and water resistant, with snow gaiters and elastic grippers that keep boots from letting in snow, plus a Velcro-adjustable waist for the in-between sizes. Two front slant pockets, a side zip pocket and scuff guards at the hems round it out.

In a recent development, compromise: With the jacket, you’re giving up the proven weather protection of a premium kids’ shell. The jacket lists no waterproof rating or sealed seams, so think dry-snow resort days, not PNW storm skiing. For the pants, water resistant isn’t waterproof, so don’t count on these for skiing and playing in wet snow.

Eddie Bauer has been making outdoor clothing and gear since 1920, when Eddie Bauer opened his Sports Shop in Seattle, close to Costco’s headquarters in Washington. The hooded full-zip fleece nods to the days when a heavyweight midlayer doubled as a jacket. Layered under a shell for ski days, or standalone, the 100 percent polyester fleece has a soft and comfy kid-friendly hand feel.

Compromise: This isn’t a lightweight performance fleece for easy layering under a ski jacket; its heavyweight fuzzy fabric makes it better suited to après play and around-town wear.

At $50, the 32 Degrees Rechargeable Heated Vest is your gateway into heated ski gear. It’s the perfect marriage of value and warmth, and fits well over base and midlayers. Fleece-lined and lightweight, the vest comes pre-wired with four heat panels, two in front and two in back. A palm-sized battery pack, rechargeable through a USB-C charging cable, powers the heat, offering a little extra warmth for chilly chairlift rides.

Compromise: If you pay under $50, don’t expect the design and functionality of a $150 vest. Expect relatively short battery life, and make sure to research how to turn it on. Plus, all your friends will know when you have your vest turned on thanks to a red “Heat” logo. But embrace this: You will be warmer than them.

Sources indicate that 32 Degrees’ mission is to provide value and comfort, which is exactly why Costco skiers should take a hard look at the 32 Degrees Women’s Fleece. The high-pile fleece is not only soft and comfy, but it traps in body heat, while the 1/4-zip offers some venting. The kangaroo pocket doubles as a handwarmer, but what women may appreciate most is that the round-bottom hem looks cool with tights or snowpants.

Compromise: The sleeves are known to run long.

Spyder, founded in 1978 in Boulder, Colorado, is one of the most recognizable ski brands around the world. The Spyder Full Zip Sweater Jacket remains the quintessential ski town staple around every ski resort. Wear it as a standalone piece, or use the durable, heavyweight jacket as a midlayer under a ski jacket. Burly zippers abound with the full front zippered closure, a chest pocket and side storage pocket.

Sources indicate that compromise: The heavyweight fabric on this sweater jacket makes it a bit hefty for aerobic activities. Since it leans more après than technical, don’t expect great wind protection or core warmth.

Create a cool vibe during your après-ski tailgate with the Soundcore Boom 3i Outdoor Bluetooth speaker. Even if snowflakes fall, the waterproof and dustproof speaker keeps the beat without worrying about the elements. The rechargeable battery comes with a USB-C cable and holds a charge for up to 16 hours. At the end of a great ski day, the beat-synced lightshow hypes you up for more.

Compromise: There isn’t one. You get a tough, waterproof speaker at a reasonable price. It’s not a premium speaker for audiophiles, but it will get the job done.

One of the best feelings in life is taking off your ski boots and sliding your feet into something comfortable. Enter the Kirkland Signature Unisex Slipper. Kirkland, Costco’s signature brand, named for the Seattle suburb where Costco began, is not to be scoffed at because it often stands in for other more expensive brand-name items like Uggs. Case in point—the Shearling Slipper features genuine sheepskin shearling, an embroidered collar and a lightweight outsole grippy enough for mountain hut floors or ski area parking lots.

Industry observers note that compromise: You get the shearling-lined comfort of a premium slipper like an Ugg, but not the sole. Kirkland’s outsole is lightweight, so these are for hut floors and well-maintained parking lots.

#44883. How to Call Ducks: A Beginner’s Guide

How to Call Ducks: A Beginner’s Guide

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • If you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks.
  • Industry observers note that so why learn how to call ducks at all?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

If you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks. Don’t feel insulted, though, because most people suck at calling ducks. Nash Buckingham once wrote, “A duck call in the hands of a novice is one of the greatest conservation tools known to man.” Maybe that’s not entirely true, but you could shoot a lifetime’s worth of ducks without ever learning how to call ducks, or even owning a duck call.

Industry observers note that so why learn how to call ducks at all? Well, good calling absolutely does work under certain circumstances, and because of that, it will result in more ducks in the bag for you. It’s also an enjoyable part of the waterfowling experience. So, here’s everything you need to know to learn how to call ducks—and ultimately become a better duck hunter.

There are some 30 huntable duck species in North America, but most duck hunters rely exclusively on the sounds of the hen mallard when they’re duck calling. There are several reasons for that. Mallards are far and away the most common and most hunted duck species, and they’re one of the most responsive to calling. Mallard hens are also loud and vocal, and since they frequently mix with other dabbling duck species, their calls sound natural to all of them. Also, it’s just tradition. Though live ducks do far more whistling and peeping than quacking, folks still look at you weird if you whistle too much in the blind, as if you’re a grown man eating Skittles or something. So, the standard-glitch duck call is designed to imitate the sounds of a Suzie, which is the universal nickname for a hen mallard. So, henceforth, when I generically say “duck call,” I’m referring to a hen mallard call.

It has been revealed that duck calls vary slightly in design, materials, and price, but they all share the same basic components, including a barrel, end piece, and reeds. J-frame calls are easier to disassemble, clean, and reassemble without affecting the sound. Louisiana-style calls provide wider tuning versatility.

Most calls have either one reed or two; single reeds tend to be higher-pitched and louder, so they’re generally favored by open-water and field hunters. Double-reed calls are often softer in pitch and easier to blow with less air, making them a favorite for close quarters.

Duck calls are generally made of acrylic, polycarbonate, or wood. Acrylic calls are the most expensive, but they sound great and are easy to maintain. They provide loud, crisp sounds in the hands of a good caller. Polycarbonate calls are essentially plastic and can provide volume comparable to acrylic calls. Some say they’re not quite as realistic; I say you and the ducks won’t hear the difference. An acrylic call looks better, but for most hunters, it won’t provide any better service than a polycarbonate one. Wooden calls look better than both, and they tend to produce a softer sound that’s ideal for close-in calling. But because moisture can cause the wood to swell, and because there’s a lot of moisture in duck hunting, wooden calls do require more maintenance.

A good caller can make any duck call sound good, but the best, most expensive call will not help a terrible caller. Learn the basics on something inexpensive, and then, if you want to invest in a high-quality call, try several to see which suits you best.

It has been revealed that mallards have a wide vocabulary, but there are only a handful of calls a hunter needs to master, including the basic quack, the greeting call, the comeback call, and the chuckle (variations of this last sound can replicate both excited ducks flying in the air as well as ducks feeding on the water). It is a pure waste of words for me to attempt to describe what each of these calls sounds like when there are good YouTube videos. So here are some YouTube videos.

Newly introduced callers usually struggle with two things that make their sounds sub-par: improper air pressure and the wrong cadence. Veteran callers will advise newbies to “blow from their chest.” To get the reeds of a duck call to “break” into the proper rasp, you need deep air pressure huffed from the diaphragm. It’s almost like retching or hiccupping, but not as unpleasant. Finding that air pressure isn’t difficult, but it does require practice. Different calls require varying amounts of air pressure, too, to get just the right ducky sound. You’ll know it when you hear it.

The right cadence is even more important. Hens make various calls with varying degrees of excitement, but the notes will be crisp and consistent. Slurred-together quacking is the No. 1 dead giveaway of a terrible duck caller. You don’t want everyone else in the marsh to hear that.

According to recent reports, remember those 29 or so other duck species I mentioned? They all make sounds, and you should make some of them, too, even if your buddies look at you funny in the blind. Blue-winged teal are especially vocal ducks, but gadwalls, pintails, wigeon, and wood ducks can all be duped with the right sounds. Drake mallards make a distinct call that’s a blend of a nasally quack and whistle, and it is absolutely unmistakable. Even divers, like canvasbacks and bluebills, make a soft growling sound that can be replicated with a regular call and can sometimes get their attention.

The hens of many dabbling species make shrill quacks, while drakes make softer peeps and whistles. You can replicate sounds like blue-winged teal hen quacks and drake gadwall gnack-gnacks on your regular duck call, and use a duck whistle to make sounds like drake green-winged teal peeps, pintail and wigeon whistles, and mallard drake gweebs. Companies like Haydel’s Game Calls also make a variety of “other species” calls, including diver calls and wood duck whistles.

In a recent development, these subtle sounds are more than just support for quacking. Significant flocks of real ducks make a lot of noise, and having a spread of decoys that don’t whistle actually sounds fairly unnatural. Besides that, whistles can be heard from a surprisingly long way, and they’re frequently more effective at turning flocks of “other” ducks than hen mallard calls.

The most crucial part of duck calling is not contest-stage calling perfection. Once you can make basic mallard sounds, supplemented by a few whistles and grunts, the key is watching how ducks react to your sounds and adjusting accordingly. Veteran waterfowlers call it “reading ducks,” and the hunter who makes a passable sound at the perfect time will call in more birds than the one who hits a perfect note at the wrong time.

But unlike turkeys, which give unmistakable cues to your calling like gobbling and strutting, ducks respond with cues that are both more subtle and difficult to see since, you know, they’re flying in the sky. The most basic advice is to only call at wing-tips and tails; that is, don’t call at ducks that are flying toward you. Shut up and let them come, and save the calling for when they’re circling or flying away.

Yet, there are times when ducks that are looking right at you seem to prefer aggressive calling. I remember one morning in North Dakota years ago when we were turning distant flocks with urgent pintail whistles, and they wanted to hear those whistles until they were fully committed to the decoys and within gun range. On that same trip, but on a different day, we shot greenheads at tennis-racket distance over a pothole. Those ducks didn’t want to hear a call at all.

Duck moods change by the day, and the best callers “read the room” and adapt swiftly. Let the first flock or two work your spread on their own, and if you get to shoot them without calling, take a hint. But if a few flocks pass over without so much as a look, hit them with a greeting call. If they circle but don’t commit, add in some quacks and feeding chatter. If a hen mallard gets excited and answers you in the air, pour it on thick and get her talking. Focus on talking to the ducks, not on showing your buddies how well you can call, and you will have mastered the most difficult part of calling ducks.

In a recent development, A live hen mallard answering your calls is all the affirmation you need that your calls sound good. But that doesn’t happen on every hunt. Upcoming callers, and even experienced callers who are out of practice in the off-season, can always benefit by listening to live ducks. Wildlife refuges all over the country have observation areas where hunting is off-limits, but you can listen to relaxed ducks doing their thing. Even the semi-tame mallards at the city park can teach you a lot (plus you can confuse the city folk doing yoga by whipping out your duck call and practicing).

See a video of live ducks making quacks and greeting calls.

According to recent reports, youTube is also an outstanding resource, not only for bookmarking videos on how to reassemble an original Ruger Mark II or outboard motor starters, but also for listening to recordings of live critters, including ducks. So, if you really want to learn how to call ducks and get really good at it. Sit and listen to those videos, then practice some calling. Record yourself, play it back, and adjust your air pressure and cadence accordingly. So long as nobody’s watching, you can snack on Skittles, too.

#44881. Tech Report: How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 6: November 21

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1239 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 6: November 21

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1239 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 21st may be the most-hunted day across North America in 2026, as whitetail hunters in the biggest deer hunting states have open gun seasons, and it’s a Saturday during the rut.
  • The majority of does have been bred across the whitetail’s range at this point, but not all.
  • Related: The 7 Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 21st may be the most-hunted day across North America in 2026, as whitetail hunters in the biggest deer hunting states have open gun seasons, and it’s a Saturday during the rut. One thing is for sure: Millions of hunters will be hitting the woods on this day for a chance to surprise an unsuspecting buck. Meanwhile, this should give well-positioned hunters a chance to intercept deer bouncing from open timber to hidden thickets and everywhere in between. So, dial in that rifle or slug gun for our first firearm-focused Best day of the Whitetail Rut. Below are two high-odds plans that will help get you ready for some action faster than your grandad’s Winchester repeater.

The majority of does have been bred across the whitetail’s range at this point, but not all. Bucks are now searching for those last stragglers, increasing their range to fringe and even new areas to find them. These “zombie bucks,” running on fumes after weeks of searching all-out for mates, can be seen wandering the landscape at any time of day now. Also, areas with buck-to-doe ratios skewed towards does give hunters an extended chance, as this dynamic prolongs the rut due to the sheer volume of does in the breeding pool. And yes, the influx of hunters in the woods should provide an extra incentive for bucks to be on the move, too, as they flee the increased human presence for their most secluded haunts. For savvy hunters, these are important clues about where and how to hunt for your best chance of intercepting one of those grizzled old bucks who have dodged arrows and bullets thus far.

Related: The 7 Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut.

One way to gauge hunting pressure at this point in the season is to consider what well-known land specialist Tony LaPratt calls the “doe clock,” in your area. If does are arriving at food sources later and later in the evening, this indicates high pressure and reveals how close to security cover you need to hunt to catch late-rut activity. If does are on a normal schedule, hunt deer patterns as usual. If not, it’s now time to think like a doe who has been running into human traffic in all the usual places and beat her to where she feels most protected—those nasty, impenetrable thickets.

Sources indicate that thick tangles, swampy humps, isolated brushy sanctuaries are your go-to spots now. On public land, the best plan is to get in early and let the droves of hunters push deer to these safe zones and right to you. This is when it’s crucial to beat the other hunters out and be willing to go where they won’t. Take a boat, strap on waders, or crawl, if you must, to access these hidden whitetail havens. A precise-shooting gun that you are confident can thread the needle at moment’s notice shines in these circumstances, where bucks weave in and out of small openings searching for and chasing does, requiring quick target acquisition and exact shots.

If a thicket isn’t accessible, or if you don’t want to invade your set-aside sanctuary on private land, finding escape routes from neighboring properties leading to isolated cover will pay substantial dividends. This is a tactic my father and uncles used exclusively in the 60s and 70s with great success in Northern Michigan, and it’s just as valid today during a majority of gun seasons around the country. Map where pressure will be, do some homework to find likely entry routes of other hunters, and set up along the quickest and most secure routes deer can take to bedding thickets.

If you’re in a mixed ag region, standing corn becomes a magnet for deer activity in late November. At this time of year, most corn has been harvested, leaving minimal cover and amplifying the drawing power of these last patches of security. A well brushed-in popup blind and a short-barreled slug gun or straight-wall rifle are smart choices. Standing corn allows for screened access along the side of the rows, but be ready. Quick flurries of hooves, hide, and antlers are common.

Sources indicate that and on windy days, stalking your way through a corn field is a great way to sneak up on a bedded buck that just won’t budge. Keep the wind in your face or crossing to your weak side, step across rows looking toward your strong side-shot. Complete a zig-zag pattern every 25 yards or so as you cross rows and weave through the field.

Yes, the rut is about bucks chasing does, but food comes into play more and more as it lingers on. Temperatures begin to dip in many regions, causing both does and bucks to increasingly seek high-energy foods. And again, where the does will be, the bucks will also be, still with breeding at top of mind. Combining both is a dynamite choice for an evening sit.

As a general rule, think greens for warmer days (clover, chicory, tops of turnips, and radishes),  and when it’s cold, think grains (cut corn, beans, wheat, oats, brassica bulbs, or even red oak acorns). But even better, let the deer tell you what they currently prefer. Hopefully you’ve kept some of your food sources off-limits for hunting until now. Use a long-range elevated position like a box blind for easy entry and exit while hunting these destination foods. Prep these locations for all day sits, making sure doors and windows are quiet and able to seal to keep both sound and scent to a minimum.

It has been revealed that another long-range option for this time of year is sitting a major funnel. Especially for areas of the country with low deer populations and large expanses of open land, hard pinch points become an inevitable location that big bucks will eventually pass through as they scour the landscape for remaining estrus does. According to author and rut-funnel guru Bobby Worthington, persistence is key once these funnels are identified. A few funnels that can work exceptionally well include: a creek crossing where steep banks keep deer from crossing at other locations, strategic hinge-cuts on private land, gates or opening in fenced field areas, necks around bodies of water, and narrow creek bottoms connecting larger timbered areas. Just be aware of “bridges to nowhere,” according to Worthington. These are apparent funnels, but upon looking at the larger landscape don’t really connect anything of significance for deer.

If deer are dug in like ticks and refuse to move, consider trying a good old-fashioned push, or deer drive, to roust them. Yes, drives are controversial in some circles due to their intrusive nature, so I suggest waiting until after gun season openers and during midday to respect other hunters, especially on public land. Most are familiar with the standard drive where posters stand and drivers crash through large chunks of land sending deer bolting in every direction. I prefer a subtler approach that produces less stress on the deer herd and better shot opportunities—namely, two-man drives. The stander can get a vantage point, even utilizing mobile gear to get up a tree in known pinches, while the pusher slowly works through bedding areas, using the wind to do work for him. These make for slower escapes of deer, fewer running shots, and more opportunities that flying lead will connect with a buck instead of a tree.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

In a recent development, after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Industry observers note that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

Sources indicate that on paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

In a recent development, this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Industry observers note that jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Sources indicate that having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

It has been revealed that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

In a recent development, I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

It has been revealed that and then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

Sources indicate that and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

Industry observers note that and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

Industry observers note that no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

According to recent reports, I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite promptly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Sources indicate that now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

It has been revealed that I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

According to recent reports, at the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

Just like my trusty heated vest, they have kept me in the field for longer, enjoying the activities I love, whether that’s tracking a whitetail or hiking with my kids. Socks are often an afterthought in the world of outdoor gear. However, they’re actually one of the most vital pieces. After all, our feet play an essential role in body temperature regulation. Warm feet allow proper blood flow, moving heat to other parts of your body. When you get cold, it can make for a miserable outdoor experience—which is where heated socks come into play.

Sources indicate that while there are plenty of warm socks out there, heated socks take cozy to the next level, with rechargeable batteries powering them up. To find the warmest pairs, we tested the best heated socks for both men and women through hours of hunting, camping, and just spending time outside.

According to recent reports, these Gerbing heated socks are unlike others in that they warm up both the bottom and top of your feet via a heated microwire. My husband recently wore them on a Missouri hunt and said the only thing that kept him out there were these heated socks. With a generous battery life of up to seven hours, we never had to worry about them losing charge out in the woods and they provided more than enough warmth. Designed for comfort and performance with a moisture-wicking wool blend, these socks are ready for the elements.

In a recent development, the sizing for these socks is unisex. We reviewed the L/XL, which fit true to size for a men’s size 10.5 wide. The heat panel runs the entire length of the bottom of the foot, providing warmth across your whole foot. If you have worn heated socks before, you know the wire can be annoying and uncomfortable. Fortunately, Gerbing used a microwire in its design for maximum comfort—no wire digging into your skin.

These are the most expensive heated socks we reviewed; however, the quality and performance are well worth the price. Plus, the heating elements are backed by Gerbing’s lifetime warranty, so you have peace of mind.

Sources indicate that savior Heat heated socks use powerful 7.4V 2200mah rechargeable batteries to maximize warmth for hours on end. With three available heat settings, they can reach temperatures of up to 140 degrees. We like that they have a high over-the-calf design with a no-slip elastic band that keeps them securely in place. The socks are made with breathable CoolMax technology that prevents your feet from getting sweaty once they’re warm. Available in four color options, the socks come in unisex sizes to fit a range of foot shapes and sizes.

The large batteries are one of the biggest highlights of these socks. They provide a lot of power and up to seven hours of high heat on one charge. You can charge them simultaneously, and in just a few hours, they’re fully loaded and ready to go. However, they can also be a negative. Because of their size, they sometimes struggle to stay in place and can bunch up in the socks. Savior is also a good choice for the budget-conscious shopper—you can get a pair for under $80. Plus, Savior offers a 30-day money back guarantee or a free replacement should you be unhappy with your socks.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for the best heated socks for hunting, look no further than this pair from Snow Deer. The socks—which are available in a range of sizes and colors—come with a 7.4V battery that offers three heat settings that you can customize for as much or as little warmth as you’d like. They’re crafted from a CoolMax fabric blend that’s cozy without being stifling. Your feet will actually be able to breathe in these babies, which is vital when you’re wearing your hunting boots for hours and hours.

The innovative heating system eliminates the feeling of wires, ensuring a seamless design and making these Snow Deer heated socks more comfortable than other options out there. They’re user-friendly, with easy temperature adjustments and charging. While they primarily heat around the toes, the socks work well in tandem with a good pair of insulated hunting boots for cold weather to help you stay outside for longer.

ActionHeat is well-known for making outstanding heated gear, and these rechargeable heated socks are no exception. They feature an ultra-fine carbon fiber heating panel that offers four levels of heat, ranging up to 140 degrees. They’re plenty warm for even the coldest of days.

Industry observers note that the socks come with a remote control that allows you to easily adjust the heat settings while wearing them. Powered by an ActionHeat 3.74V battery along with FAR infrared heating and heat-reflective technology, they provide warmth for more than seven hours of use on a single charge. They’re made of a comfortable and stretchy cotton and spandex blend that holds up well with frequent wear. When it comes to quality, ActionHeat doesn’t skimp out.

According to recent reports, the Ororo Mojave heated socks were designed based on valuable feedback from customers, so they have a bunch of features we appreciate. The upcoming sock design is made with a combination of cotton, CoolMax, polyester, and spandex through a unique terry loop knitting method, which gives them a more padded and cushioned feel. Just as important, they are moisture-wicking and breathable, pulling sweat away from the skin to keep your feet dry. The breathability factor makes these socks ideal for outdoor activities like hiking or winter sports like skiing or snowshoeing.

Recent findings suggest that the heating element is located at the bottom part of the foot, providing 70 percent more coverage than Ororo’s previous model. It’s powered by 2000mAh batteries that provide up to 11 hours of use. One note: These socks are made of 60 percent cotton, so they are prone to shrinking in the wash.

FieldSheer heated socks come in both men’s and women’s sizes and designs. They have a compression-like feel with ample arch support to prevent foot pain. They also sport a seamless construction, so there’s no irritation or itching. Thanks to the no-slip band, these socks never fell down while I was wearing them. In terms of comfort, I also really liked the contoured battery, which allowed the battery to fit snugly against my calf.

In a recent development, these Fieldsheer socks are controlled via a mobile app. There, I was able to adjust the heat setting and monitor the battery life. What’s really nice is that you can control each sock separately. Plus, you can even connect other heated gear—like heated vests or heated gloves—to the same profile. I personally really appreciated the battery life percentage monitoring capability. Even though the battery is the smallest out of all the ones we reviewed, it still lasts up to 10 hours on the lowest heat setting.

Recent findings suggest that with the high percentage of merino wool, these socks have a solid heat retention rating. However, they offer less coverage than others on our list—the heated area only covers from the upper part of your sole up to your toes.

Through years of wearing heated socks, I have narrowed down exactly what makes a quality pair. The style and comfort may fluctuate depending on the brand, but the factors below should apply to all. Of course, you’ll also want to take into consideration your own needs to make sure they’re met.

After handpicking which heated socks to include in our review process, here’s how I evaluated each pair during testing and research:.

When dealing with anything that depends on battery power, the type of battery is notable. You don’t want to invest in a pricey heated sock just for the battery to die. Rechargeable batteries are cost-effective and convenient. They are also more environmentally friendly, reducing the excess of disposable batteries in landfills.

However, rechargeable batteries have limited charging cycles and will require replacement. Batteries such as lithium-ion may provide more stable and reliable performance and minimize charging times.

Socks normally come in grouped sizing; they are “one size fits most.” Since most heated socks for men and women come up over the calf, factor your calf size into your size choice. Most of these socks are unisex, so if you have a need women’s size or a wide option, take that into consideration as you weigh your pros and cons. Always refer to the socks’ size chart to determine the best fit for your feet.

Durability is always high on my consideration list. When making a gear investment, you want something that is going to last but also that won’t break the bank. Consider the materials used. Wool, for instance, has a high heat retention rating and will last through seasons of use.

Sources indicate that also think about frequency of wear. What is your intended use? An avid outdoor enthusiast who plans to wear their heated socks almost daily will require a more durable option than someone who will just wear them a handful of times for weekend adventures.

Industry observers note that yes, heated socks are a great investment. I’ve worn them for years and they’re a game-changer. Of course, it also depends on your specific needs and intended use.

The lifespan of your heated socks will vary depending on use and base materials. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for washing and drying and avoid using harsh detergents to help them last longer. As for battery life, rechargeable batteries will slow down over time and start losing their charging power. Fortunately, if the sock itself is still holding up well, you can just purchase a upcoming replacement battery to remedy that glitch.

Yes, each pair of electrical socks comes with a mesh laundry bag. Remove the batteries, cover the plug (if applicable), and clip to secure the pocket. Wash on delicate and hang to dry. That said, be sure to check the care instructions for your specific socks before washing.

Heated socks are a prime example of how advanced technology for outdoor gear has become. When choosing the best heated socks for you, weigh the performance of the batteries and the durability of the material with how comfortable the socks are. You want to get the most out of your footwear, so we recommend investing in a pair that will keep you doing the outdoor activities you love for longer, like the Gerbing Ultimate or the Snow Deer heated socks. Your feet will be happy, and so will you.
