UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28.
  • There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running.
  • One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

For the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:.

Recent findings suggest that race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Recent findings suggest that two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI confirmed the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”.

Recent findings suggest that the discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its newly introduced mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

Industry observers note that the 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

Recent findings suggest that this will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

It has been revealed that from the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti says. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”.

According to recent reports, but coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Industry observers note that keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he states.

Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB. “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”.

Industry observers note that american Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”.

In a recent development, if there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne said.

For spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”.

Industry observers note that could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Sources indicate that doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour tech giant Run the Alps.

Breaking: Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

  • It has been revealed that “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

According to recent reports, audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing new climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

It has been revealed that “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

“With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” mentioned Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

According to recent reports, pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

According to recent reports, pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

11 Climber Gift Ideas You Probably Haven’t Thought of Yet, According to Editors

💡 Key Takeaways

  • (Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your latest boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

Originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk showed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

Sources indicate that luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

In a recent development, for climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

It has been revealed that the fresh Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

It has been revealed that the Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

Sources indicate that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

It has been revealed that the pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the new film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

The oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

According to recent reports, note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a latest collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

Tech Report: A Climber We Lost: Jun Kyu Kim

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell.
  • Industry observers note that born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters.
  • Jun once stated that climbing was the thing he lived for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Industry observers note that born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which quickly became his true passion.

Jun once stated that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

According to recent reports, I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee claims that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

It has been revealed that jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly released Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

According to recent reports, that was Jun—a man with an unbelievably big heart who was always looking for a way to help and who highlighted up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

Climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m.
  • In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

Sources indicate that “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

According to recent reports, as many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

It has been revealed that junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram indicates the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

In a recent development, “Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

In a recent development, according to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video demonstrates the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

In an interview with The Gazette, Talley said, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

Authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF stated that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate intends to avoid the area.”.

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website indicates no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

In a recent development, outside of Colorado, New Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

It has been revealed that while the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

According to recent reports, “While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

Grand Theft Auto 6 Has an Entire National Park. I Spent the Night Exploring It.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.
  • Recent findings suggest that many gamers have waited 13 years for a new Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city.
  • Sources indicate that GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.

Recent findings suggest that many gamers have waited 13 years for a new Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city. I had a slightly different mission. I wanted to go hiking.

Sources indicate that GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida. Beyond the game’s cities and beaches are mangrove swamps, forested mountains, and a surprising number of opportunities for outdoor recreation.

Among them is an entire national park that some fans believe was inspired by Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park. Naturally, as a journalist who covers the outdoors, I decided to investigate.

Industry observers note that getting there was its own expedition. I spent several hundred dollars on a PlayStation 5 specifically for this assignment, endured a download that initially threatened to take 14 hours, and worked through introductory missions involving a robbery and a dubious boating operation before I could drive north to the game’s national park—Mount Kalaga.

In a recent development, located near Leonida’s northern border, Mount Kalaga is one of six major regions players can explore, with a vast stretch of mountainous backcountry offering hunting, fishing, and off-road trails, according to Rockstar’s official description. It took me about 20 minutes of real-life driving to get there from the game’s starting point, though my tendency to crash into medians at full speed probably added a few minutes to the trip.

According to recent reports, mount Kalaga isn’t especially faithful to real-world park rules. Hunting is generally prohibited in U.S. national parks unless specifically authorized, while off-road vehicle use is restricted. Still, the park’s layout, scenery, and recreation options reflect an impressive effort to make the fictional outdoors feel like somewhere worth visiting.

In a recent development, the drive into the park looks a lot like Northern California, with winding roads cutting through steep, lush hillsides. Farther in, the landscape opens up to waterfalls, rocky cliffs, and wide waterways bordered by dense vegetation, with forested islands and bridges stretching across the valleys below.

According to recent reports, more impressive than the landscape was how well the game designers captured the everyday details of an actual national park. They included designated trailheads, road markers, and even went so far as to build public restrooms that look unpleasantly familiar to anyone who’s ever used the real deal. The park also has a visitor center with a wooden porch, green railings, tourists milling around outside, and a sign above the entrance reading, “True wanderers are never lost.”.

It holds far more wildlife than I managed to spot in one visit, too. Rockstar told gaming publication Game Informer that Leonida contains more than 170 animal species, and The Guardian reported that players can identify 62 types of birds using binoculars and record them in a wildlife logbook.

Inside Mount Kalaga National Park, I found designated hiking trails dotted with wildflowers and packed with both sporty dog walkers and out-of-breath tourists alike, alongside an elaborate, technical mountain bike trail system. Complete with marked access routes, wooden bridges, and built-out ramps and drops, it looked like a legitimate, and genuinely difficult, trail network, with a time-trial mode built in for players looking to race the course.

I acquired my mountain bike in a way that probably wouldn’t go over well at an actual trailhead; I stole it from a group of unsuspecting riders taking in the view of the lower valley.

After exploring on foot and two wheels and evading a gaggle of angry policemen looking for a bike thief, I paddled a red kayak through a wooded waterway and took a park-service-looking off-road vehicle onto the dirt roads.

Next, I decided to hot-wire a vacant ATV from a trailhead parking lot and set off on a backcountry joyride. From an overlook, I watched rivers wind between tree-lined islands as the sun set, and later, at the top of Mount Kalaga, I looked up at a sky full of stars as the sound of crickets drifted out of the game and into my living room.

What began with a frantic search for the last PlayStation 5 in stock at Target and a virtual armed robbery, ended with a peaceful evening in what might be the most meticulously detailed national park ever created for a video game.

#44834. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4447 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

These nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Industry observers note that ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

Sources indicate that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Concerns with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Sources indicate that firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “blueprint falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

In a recent development, what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

According to recent reports, if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

Industry observers note that the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

For maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

Recent findings suggest that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Recent findings suggest that have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

In a recent development, if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

Sources indicate that the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

The most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

The quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

Industry observers note that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Sources indicate that once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

Recent findings suggest that the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Recent findings suggest that now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

Recent findings suggest that if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

Industry observers note that if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

According to recent reports, even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid substantial swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Sources indicate that besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

It has been revealed that on coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

Sources indicate that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done quickly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

In a recent development, technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a massive, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is key.

Recent findings suggest that lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that but, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

In a recent development, if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

It has been revealed that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

It has been revealed that while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Sources indicate that let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a new stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

Recent findings suggest that but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is important. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

According to recent reports, if the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

If the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

Recent findings suggest that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

Industry observers note that speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

According to recent reports, I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

It has been revealed that see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

The 9 Best Snowshoes of 2027

Industry observers note that L.L. Bean Pathfinder BOA Rec Snowshoe Package.

Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes.

After a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip. Looking for a crazy-affordable pair that will last for years? The Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes ($50-70) are nearly bulletproof, easy to manipulate with gloves on, and provide a full feature set. This year we added the L.L. Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

Sources indicate that snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

Sizes: 22, 25 in Weight: Men’s: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4.1 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 3.6 lbs (22 in), 3.9 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: Men’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 220 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 lbs (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Easy-to-engage heel lift + Very secure binding – Pricey.

The Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s new binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she mentioned.

Sizes: 20.5, 22.5, 26.5 in Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5), 3.8 lbs (22.5), 4lbs (26.5) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (22.5 in), 300 lbs (26.5 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Comfortable stride + Tall heel lift – Expensive.

It has been revealed that the Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of newly introduced snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

Sources indicate that sizes: 25, 30, 36 in. (men’s) 21, 25 (women’s) Weight: 4.9 lbs (25 in), 5.6 lbs (30 in), 6.5 lbs (36 in) Maximum Load: 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 280 lbs (36 in).

Pros and Cons + Great traction on hills + Easy to adjust, glove-friendly binding + Wide range of sizes – Wider decks can be cumbersome.

Sources indicate that L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging quickly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a major plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

On a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Sizes: 22, 25 in. Weight: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Good traction on slopes + Easy-to-use binding + Heel lift – Expensive.

It has been revealed that many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too massive for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

Sizes: 20.5, 23.5, 27 in. Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5 in), 3.8 lbs (23.5 in), 4 lbs (27 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (23.5 in), 300 lbs (27 in).

Pros and Cons + Intuitive BOA system + Multi-direction crampons + Flexible + Heel lift – Expensive – No tail extensions – Not great in powder.

For those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Easy-to-use BOA-style bindings – Below-average traction – No heel lift.

Over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of latest snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Sizes: 21, 25, and 30 in. Weight: 4 lbs (21 in), 4.2 lbs (25 in), 4.8 lbs (30 in) Maximum Load: 120-250 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

According to recent reports, the double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Sources indicate that our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Pros and Cons + One size fits all + Affordable + Impressive traction + Float tail-compatible – No heel lift.

In a recent development, described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

It has been revealed that the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

It has been revealed that the Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of new snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

The Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

Flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

According to recent reports, on the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are crucial for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

According to recent reports, in deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or plan to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

According to recent reports, over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

We looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like new bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Kristin Smith A former Backpacker editor, category manager Kristin Smith has been a full- or part-time mountain guide for most of the last decade. In her spare time, she teaches Avalanche Terrain Avoidance for the Colorado Mountain Club, guides clients through the nearby peaks of Rocky Mountain National Park, and maps out new places to visit with her recently-acquired pilot’s license.

Industry observers note that jill Yarger Jill Yarger works as a mountain guide in Boulder, Colorado. She moved for an engineering job, found the mountains, and never left; that was almost 40 years ago. Since then she’s spent 13 years volunteering in the Rocky Mountain Rescue Group, joined the National Ski Patrol and Mountain Rescue Associations, and climbed in Alaska, Italy, and Canada.

Jessica Bucklin Jessica Bucklin spent a decade sailing tall ships all over the world before moving to the coast of Maine, where finding enough snow to snowshoe often requires just a walk down the road. When she’s not exploring Maine’s mountain parks she captains a towboat out of Bath.

Joe O’Leary Joe’s guiding career spanned North, Central, and South America before he settled in Colorado, where he now trains other guides in whitewater rafting, mountain biking, backpacking, and leadership development.
