💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in New York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • The day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in New York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

The day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

It has been revealed that upcoming York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

Sources indicate that but time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with looks to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

According to recent reports, when the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

Finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

“This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch remarked that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

In a recent development, “It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch said. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

According to recent reports, the hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

Recent findings suggest that people with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, mentioned there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

Recent findings suggest that “In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly says. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

Wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he says SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody promptly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

He states e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Industry observers note that urgency is particularly vital in these cases, Cooper notes. Research shows that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper notes, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

#44809. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1323 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good manufacturer.”.

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Right now, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her significant three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

In a recent development, when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

Sources indicate that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we promptly got all our stuff together.

We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

Industry observers note that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

It has been revealed that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

So she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Sources indicate that will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Recent findings suggest that every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he said it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

In a recent development, I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

Recent findings suggest that it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a massive light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

In a recent development, lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Upcoming York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

  • It has been revealed that authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
  • Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe. Since 2022, at least 28 pines have been harmed or destroyed, totaling $300,000 in damages, authorities noted in a release.

Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.

Recent findings suggest that “We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” Sheriff Darin Balaam stated in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.

In an email to Outside, WCSO spokesperson Rachel Piccinini mentioned the agency is continuing to investigate the crimes, which could result in felony charges.

“Our office has received numerous tips from the community, and we continue to encourage anyone with information that may assist in this investigation to contact our Detective Division,” Piccinini remarked.

According to recent reports, outside requested further information about whether the incidents pose a threat to people or pets recreating in the area. We will update this article if we receive a response.

Recent findings suggest that the tree poisonings have occurred at Burnt Cedar Beach, a lakefront recreation complex in Incline Village, Nevada, along Lake Tahoe’s north shore. It’s also about a ten-minute drive from the community-owned Diamond Peak Ski Resort. Roughly 9,000 people live in Incline Village, but the area is a tourism hotspot in both winter and summer.

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years. Authorities say they believe the same person damaged all the trees. The suspect harmed the first six in 2022 and another six in 2024.

It has been revealed that most recently, on July 24, 2026, deputies responded to Burnt Cedar Beach after reports of a strong odor near the base of a large pine tree. The smell matched previous tree poisonings at the property. On August 2, deputies found another tree with a substance around the base; at the time, a trail camera captured a bright light near the area at 2 A.M.

At least 16 trees were damaged in 2026 as a result.

Recent findings suggest that in some instances, someone poured the toxin directly over the tree’s base. In others, someone drilled holes near the roots and poured the substance in them.

Authorities say they have yet to identify the contaminant or determine why someone targeted the trees. They have collected soil samples and submitted them for testing. They hope to identify the substance used and determine whether the perpetrator used the same one in each incident.

WCSO asks anyone with information to call (775) 328-3001 and reference case number 26-4225.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, nine years later, Massive Bend is still beautiful.
  • One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: kellyvandellen/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that the first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S. and Mexico, I was amazed not just at how beautiful it was, but how peaceful. The buff and black-streaked limestone walls soared 1,500 feet over the water, the afternoon sun streaming through the gap. The river was running low and slow, trickling over the mud and rocks, no more than knee deep. I rolled up my pant legs and waded into the water, toward that invisible line in the middle of the river that split two countries.

According to recent reports, nine years later, Massive Bend is still beautiful. Covering an area bigger than Rhode Island, this stretch of West Texas desert is home to some of the state’s most moving scenery, from river canyons to rocky peaks, with animal and plant life to match. Hikers willing to put in the work on the area’s rugged trails may spot javelinas rooting in the undergrowth or nocturnal, raccoon-like ringtails climbing up the cliffs and trees of the Chisos Mountains; they’ll see prickly pear cactus and ocotillo, a spindly, Seussian shrub equipped with vicious spines, growing wild in the desert flats. (That border, however, may soon be far more concrete. Read on for more on that.).

One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak. At 7,825 feet, Emory is the highest point in Substantial Bend and the Chisos, and enjoys commanding views of the terrain for miles around. Getting there, however, takes some muscle: The rough, 9.7-mile hike to the top ascends singletrack and rock stairs through oak, piñon, and juniper forest before ending with a final, dramatic scramble to the peak’s exposed summit. November, when summer’s broiling temperatures finally cool down, is an ideal time to hike it. (Note: There is no water at all along the Emory Peak Trail, and the NPS suggests hikers carry at least one liter per person per hour.).

The round trip takes about 6 to 8 hours, and you’ll want to leave some time to relax afterward. Santa Elena Canyon’s picnic area is an ideal spot for an early dinner, and cap off the night at the park’s free riverside hot springs. (Due to recent flood damage, reaching both of these highlights is right now harder than usual. The paved road between Cottonwood Campground and Santa Elena is closed at the time of writing; drivers with a true 4-wheel drive vehicle and high clearance can get there on Old Maverick Road. Due to another closure, getting to the hot springs requires a 4-mile round-trip, relatively flat hike along a gravel road. Consider it part of the adventure.).

Starting at the Chisos Basin Visitors Center, take the Laguna Meadows trail for about a third of a mile to a fork, where you’ll hang a left on the Pinnacles Trail. Follow it as it steadily climbs, traversing desert flats and rocky slopes with the sheer top of Emory looming in the background. After another 3.4 miles, the trail reaches a saddle below the top of the peak. Continue on the Emory Peak Trail for another 1.5 miles, then tackle a final, somewhat exposed 30-foot scramble to the top of the mountain and 360-degree views of the park below. Retrace your steps to the trailhead, or break up the hike by reserving one of the Pinnacles campsites ahead of your trip.

According to recent reports, in an 8-1 decision on November 9, the Supreme Court approved a request by the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall through Big Bend, ruling against plaintiffs who had argued that the barrier would decimate rare plant species and cut off migratory routes for animals, and that it risked damaging ancient rock art and Native heritage sites. In Santa Elena Canyon itself, the Department of Homeland Security prepares to install vehicle barriers and surveillance infrastructure and clear patrol roads through the area. Conservation groups and state officials like Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa say they’ll continue to push to end construction in the park.

#44804. The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)

The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wilderness explorer C.
  • In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana.
  • “On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wilderness explorer C. Thomas Biscardi, who spent nearly a decade searching for Bigfoot, claimed he photographed the elusive creature during an expedition in Northern California (Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images).

In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana. At the time, he and three other hunters went into the woods to pack out a six-point bull elk they had shot down.

“On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.

At first, the men guessed a large bear had eaten the elk—but the tracks appeared in sets of two, and bears don’t tend to walk on their hind legs.

“Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear off the ground,” Kinney continued.

According to recent reports, the men followed the tracks for about a half-mile and, according to Kinney’s account, came across a felled log measuring three feet in diameter. They could see where the elk’s horns had been dragged across the snow and over the timber.

“At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was,” Kinney wrote. “Though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”.

The following year, another person, W.W. Schmitz, was hunting in a nearby area called Bills Creek when he found the same type of tracks, smelled a similarly strong odor, and also heard grunting noises.

According to recent reports, kinney’s story is one of three historical files the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) released on October 15, describing Bigfoot encounters in Washington, Oregon, and Montana. In a world rife with sasquatch hunters and Bigfoot believers, the newly unveiled reports are shedding light on a long-held conspiracy theory. The public can access the files through the USFS website.

About 70 miles away in Plains, Montana, locals described an equally bizarre Bigfoot encounter in a January 15, 2003, article published by the Clark Fork Valley Press. According to the story, around January 3, hundreds of large, human-like footprints appeared in fresh snow outside Jim Rohweder’s sawmill shop. His neighbor, Bob Mesing, reportedly measured the prints at 16.5 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with visible toes, an arch, and a stride that spanned about five feet.

Mesing and Dean Peterson, a former Kalispell policeman, followed the tracks about 100 yards into the woods, where the trail eventually faded.

It has been revealed that “I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” Mesing reportedly noted. “What else could it be?”.

According to the Clark Fork Valley Press, the men did not contact authorities but had planned to give a sample to wildlife officials.

It has been revealed that mesing mentioned he believed the visitor walked up to the shop and turned back, startled by a motion-sensor light. Peterson reportedly added that his dog barked around 3:40 A.M. that day, but he saw nothing.

Rohweder’s wife, Gladys, claimed to have seen a hairy, two-legged creature when the couple first moved to the area.

A June 16, 1982, account published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture took place in Umatilla National Forest, which hugs the southern border of Washington State and northern Oregon. In it, wildlife biologist Rodney Johnson reports that the agency asked him to investigate three sets of Bigfoot tracks and record the details of his trips.

The tracks were recorded in three locations of the Mill Creek Watershed, a 36.5-mile tributary of the Walla Walla River about 262 miles from Portland.

Site A contained six identifiable tracks going down a muddy trail for about 25 feet. Similar tracks were also seen at a second location near a bog, Site B, this time 18 prints spanning about 40 feet.

Johnson took photos and plaster casts of both sites, but skipped the third, citing terrain challenges.

But was it actually Bigfoot? Likely not.

“It is my opinion that the tracks observed at Site ‘A’ and Site ‘B’ along Low Creek were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus two-footed being,” Johnson wrote.

It has been revealed that when a two-legged being walks, its stride changes with gradient—shorter uphill and longer downhill. According to Johnson, the distance between the tracks remained a consistent four feet and did not change with the slope. The tracks also had a clear beginning and end, rather than following an existing trail. Furthermore, Johnson added that the imprints did not resemble an authentic print—for example, a human footprint shows a distinct significant toe pad and typically exhibits heel slippage on a steep gradient.

What’s more, at certain points, it appeared that pine needles had been intentionally brushed aside before the track was made.

According to recent reports, “It was obvious that the litter had been displaced sideways from the track area in an unnatural manner,” Johnson wrote. “If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow on the mountains above Rollins Pass, Colorado. (Photo: SWKrullImaging via Getty).

A late fall hike turned into an overnight rescue on the Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail on November 14 when a trio of hikers called for a rescue after encountering severe weather and wintry conditions at 11,600 feet.

Recent findings suggest that located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet. When hiked in its entirety, it also involves 3,742 feet of elevation gain over the course of 18 miles. Recent day-time temperature highs in the area have hovered between 26 and 37 degrees, while lows were recorded at 5 and 9 degrees with wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

According to recent reports, grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR), which responded, remarked that the hikers called for help after encountering dangerous trail conditions, significant snow, and navigational struggles. The team dispatched a group of rescuers who rode ATVs up the Rollins Pass Road before dismounting and hiking the remaining distance there. When rescuers made it to the trio, they found the hikers were wet, cold, and tired.

“The subjects had set up camp but lacked appropriate gear, including fire making supplies, to spend the night in the deteriorating weather,” rescue officials wrote. A second rescue team joined the party later in the evening before accompanying the hikers back to the staged ATVs and from there to the trailhead.

Although most of Grand County has yet to see significant snow, November can be a deceptive time of the year to hike in Colorado’s high country. Trails may appear accessible, but factors like extreme temperatures, inclement weather and reduced daylight hours can make hiking and camping more treacherous than usual.

In a recent development, the Continental Divide Trail is the highest-elevation long trail in the United States, with its high point at the summit of 14,278-foot Grays Peak. Colorado’s section is the highest on the trail; the USFS estimates that the CDT’s average elevation across the state is 10,000 feet.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • We love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by Newly introduced Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

We love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

According to recent reports, paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Sources indicate that insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

In a recent development, print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Sources indicate that once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

It has been revealed that then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Breaking: Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (304 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • It has been revealed that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

It has been revealed that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential challenges.

It has been revealed that honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

Latest Update: 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • Recent findings suggest that the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more key to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less notable than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy claims. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

Recent findings suggest that the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

Industry observers note that 3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up notes, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

According to recent reports, 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

According to recent reports, 6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

Industry observers note that 7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

Sources indicate that for parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

Industry observers note that 10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

It has been revealed that 11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

Sources indicate that 13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

Industry observers note that 15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

Sources indicate that 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a new way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

Industry observers note that 17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

Sources indicate that 18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

According to recent reports, for activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

Recent findings suggest that 19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

It has been revealed that 21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

It has been revealed that I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

Industry observers note that 2. Strategy a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

According to recent reports, 4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

Sources indicate that 5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

Sources indicate that 6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Major Moon.

7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

Sources indicate that 9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

Sources indicate that 11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

Industry observers note that 16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

Sources indicate that 17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

Sources indicate that 18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

Sources indicate that 20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

Recent findings suggest that 21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

According to recent reports, 22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

Recent findings suggest that 23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

It has been revealed that 24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

Recent findings suggest that 25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

It has been revealed that 28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

Industry observers note that 30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

In a recent development, 32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

Sources indicate that 33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

It has been revealed that 35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

According to recent reports, 36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

It has been revealed that 37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

According to recent reports, 39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”.

Industry observers note that 40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

Recent findings suggest that 41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them. Whether you resort to a countdown timer or go the “this is your last show” route, it’s pretty much always a struggle.

Industry observers note that perhaps you need a fresh strategy. Parenting coach Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.

Sources indicate that A few things to note about this method. Using language like “We have one more song” instead of “This is our last song before we leave for school” focuses on what the child is doing now versus what you are doing in the future. It’s easier for kids to accept the transition this way.

“Melodic intonation” is when you use a sing-songy voice to make a statement. It helps kids notice what you are saying and acknowledge it. Take a look at Miss Rachel and a lot of the other preschool-focused programming, and you’ll see it employed often. Using melodic intonation for the phrase “iPad is all done” helps to signal the transition for the child.

According to recent reports, it’s key to remember that even when using a technique like this, it will take you doing it the same way over and over several times before your child catches on and gets with the program. If they have a meltdown, don’t engage; stay calm; and move on.

15 Fun Games for Toddlers (Because You Need to Keep Them Busy)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs).
  • Sources indicate that toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning.
  • Recent findings suggest that figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs). To keep them out of trouble and thoroughly entertained, we’ve rounded up some awesome games for toddlers that are sure to be a hit, whether you’re indoors or outdoors. The best part? Your kiddo won’t know it, but they offer ample opportunities for hands-on learning. Ready for endless fun? On your mark. Get set. Go find your tot’s upcoming fave!

Sources indicate that toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning. Learning with play is essential for their development because it improves small and large motor skills, muscle strength, emotional intelligence, language development, spatial awareness, and more. According to an article by Michael Yogman, MD, FAAP, on Healthychildren.org, “research demonstrates play can improve children’s abilities to plan, organize, get along with others, and regulate emotions. In addition, play helps with language, math, and social skills, and even helps children cope with stress.”.

Recent findings suggest that figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat. There are outdoor games, indoor games, toys, beginner board games… You get the idea. The key is to decide which activity is right for your kiddo, and that depends on factors like their age, energy level, developmental stage, and other milestones.

One of the most important things to consider is what interests your toddler. Do they love Ms. Rachel? Are they obsessed with a sport? Do they love baby dolls or animals? Once you figure out what will keep them interested, you can go from there.

According to recent reports, another factor is something called Play Schemas, a concept first used by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget. As stated in My Play Cupboard, Play Schemas are repeated patterns of behaviour you notice children engaging in when they play. Nine schemas can be commonly observed in young children, including connection, transforming, enveloping, enclosing, and positioning.

Once you figure out which Play Schema your toddler is drawn to, that will help you decide what type of games they’ll enjoy the most.

Recent findings suggest that give your jumping bean something to jump about—letters! We love that this outdoor game from The Imagination Tree combines alphabet awareness with the chance to get those wiggles out. Simply write letters in sidewalk chalk and have your little one hop from one to another as you call them out. And all you need to get started is a set of sidewalk chalk. Read all about it and check out the phonics and math variations over at The Imagination Tree.

Sources indicate that let your toddler be your boss with a few rounds of Simon Indicates. Toddlers love the chance to be in charge! Then, you can give the commands for a bit. It's silly, active, and engaging—that's why it's an early childhood classic. Plus, it gives little ones a chance to practice following instructions, taking turns, and building listening skills. Simon Says go play!

It has been revealed that toddlers love climbing under, over, and on top of all sorts of things. Obstacle courses let you take that natural climbing instinct and make it a game. Build an indoor obstacle course with painters' tape, making lines for your little one to walk on top of and jump over. Or take the fun outside and challenge them to stay off the grass in the yard or the wood chips at the playground. Ready for a bonus round? Turn the obstacle course game into follow-the-leader and take turns being the leader. Check out this post for even more obstacle course fun.

It has been revealed that kids of all ages love a good scavenger hunt. Send your toddler on a hunt through the house for four red things or two things with wheels. If you have a little more time or an older toddler ready for a challenge, print out a scavenger hunt like these. Good news: they're all free!

It has been revealed that we love the Easy Boat Activity from Toddler Approved because it's budget-friendly, and it uses supplies you've already got in the house, like plastic containers, tape, and straws. Kids love it because it offers indoor water fun and the chance to capsize a fleet of tiny ships. Sail down to Toddler Approved to find out how you can set up your own version. Don't miss Kristina's ideas about what to talk about with your little one as you play to turn this game into a toddler-friendly science experiment.

Whether it's Five Little Monkeys or Ram Sam Sam, toddlers dig a good tune. Plus, rhymes and songs like these are more than just fun. They build toddlers' vocabulary and pre-literacy skills. Find new ones to add to your repertoire at Storyblocks, a site created by Colorado librarians to share rhymes and songs for toddlers and preschoolers.

Toddlers go gaga over games that give them a chance to put stuff in a container and then dump it out, so this Oatmeal Container Straw Game from Merriment Designs is bound to be a hit. We love that this game made out of recycled materials packs a massive dose of fun on a budget. Round up straws and an empty oats container, then head over to Merriment Designs to find out how to make your own.

If your toddler is anything like ours, Mama Papa Bubba's DIY Felt Board is bound to be a substantial hit because it's all about ice cream. Felt ice cream, that is. Little ones can practice fine motor skills and learn about colors as they match each colorful scoop and dot. Plus, when you've had your fill of ice cream, the board makes a perfect background for felt animals or people that can be used for storytelling fun. The possibilities are endless! Find the step-by-step instructions to create your own felt board at Mama Puppa Bubba.

Stretch it out and play a game of animal yoga with your little one. You can pick up a set of soft yoga blocks that toddlers can toss up in the air before diving into a downward-facing dog. Or try out these five animal yoga poses and pretend to be stretching tigers and rolling bears.

Recent findings suggest that eeBoo's Life on Earth has everything we look for in a memory game: sturdy pieces, beautiful eye-catching images, and the chance for game-playing fun. If your kiddo isn't quite ready to play a full game, pull out a smaller set of matching cards for mini-memory fun. Plus, talking about the pictures on the cards is a guaranteed vocabulary builder.

Available at amazon.com, $21.99.

Try the dress-up challenge: give your toddler a scenario or career, like summertime, rainy day, forest animal friends, sports star, or construction worker, and send them off to create an outfit that meets that challenge. They can use their own clothes or dig things out of the dress-up bin. Then, put on a tune that goes along with the scenario you've picked and put on a fashion show. We guarantee that you'll get lots of fantastic photos out of this game! It's also great to play after dinner to encourage little ones to put on their PJs. Last challenge: bedtime!

Most board games are still a little tricky for young toddlers—but Where's Bear from Peaceable Kingdom is just right. Little ones get to play hide-and-seek with little bear, stack the sturdy cardboard blocks, and learn new words as they play.

Available at amazon.com, $24.95.

Industry observers note that even if it's raining cats and dogs, your toddler can play Melissa and Doug's bowling game for hours. The weighted bottoms on the six soft animal pins make them easy to stand up, and the set comes with a carrying case for on-the-go fun and storage. Kiddos will build their gross motor skills and can also practice counting the pins one by one. Strike!

Available at amazon.com, $32.99.

In a recent development, caught waiting in line or at a restaurant without a stocked bag of goodies? Then pull out the animal guessing game, a game we love because it requires no gear. Think of an animal and ask questions until your game playing buddy guesses it. Does it have legs? Does it live in a tree? Older twos and three-year-olds love this game. When you're playing with younger toddlers, change it to the animal sounds game: make a sound (MOOO!) and have the toddler guess what kind of animal makes that noise. Then switch it up and have them make the sound.

Sources indicate that your toddler will spend lots of time spelling their name and piecing together words with this Magnetic Rainbow Busy Box from Mama.Papa.Bubba. It can be an art project just to create the box and they'll have endless fun learning and spelling once it's finished.

What are the benefits of toddler games?

Playing games with your toddler is not only a great opportunity to enjoy quality time with your child, but they help develop key life skills like problem solving, small and large motor skills, physical coordination, hand-eye coordination, and learning how to be social with others.

What types of games are best for toddlers?

Recent findings suggest that while it depends on your child’s age, interests, and development, the best toddler games are simple and fun. Popular ideas include pretend play, memory games, music games, and basic movements, like a simplified version of Simon Claims.

How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers?

According to the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, toddlers should have very limited daily screen time.

Recent findings suggest that there are online toddler games that are designed specifically for young children. Parents should always review the game or content before allowing their child to watch, monitor usage, and opt for an ad-free, child-friendly tablet or platform.

What are some fun indoor games for toddlers?

Toddler indoor games should be fun and easy to set up: memory, obstacle courses, block building challenges, sensory stations, and pretend play like “the floor is lava,” “vet clinic,” and “grocery store.”.

Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we are walking between two tractors in a barn when I say something very stupid to my 22-month-old son. We’ve been at this farm for about an hour, the kind of place where you can reach your fingers through the fence to pet the goats and stare into the pigpen and marvel at how much bigger pigs are than you think. It’s a mysteriously warm winter day, and my son has thrown his jacket off, his stroller discarded somewhere around the sheep pen. For the first time in months, we are feeling the sun on our faces. He’s having the time of his life. He’s already pet a one-day-old lamb and has discovered that in the barn we are currently walking through there’s not one, not two, but three tractors.

And then I decide to say, “Do you think the cat is in here today?”.

Last time we were here in the fall, there was a substantial, gray cat who got just close enough so that my toddler could bend down, reach out the tips of his fingers, and briefly graze its arched back. But that was enough. He’d brought up the cat for days, and I knew if he saw it again, he’d be so, so happy.

Except there was one problem. The cat wasn’t here.

Why did I have to mention the cat? It was a perfect moment; we were like an illustration from a children’s picture book. But now, there was only one thing my son wanted to do: find the cat. I’d reminded him that there was a cat. And he loves cats. Especially this cat, the famed cat that let him touch its fur for a fraction of a second. So of course, in a very cat-like fashion, the cat was nowhere to be found.

In a recent development, that’s when the tears began. The three tractors were no longer enough. The baby goats—garbage. The teeny tiny lambs, only minutes ago, he was thrilled to pet. Who needs them? It was only the cat now.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t know,” I mentioned, hoping his outburst wasn’t calling too much attention to us from the less cat-obsessed farm visitors. “He’s probably sleeping somewhere.”.

“WHERE CAT,” he demanded, over and over again.

And just like that, I’d broken my own biggest rule of parenting: Never try to make a happy kid happier.

Industry observers note that this rule came to me via my friend Joanna, who had learned it from her parents. As soon as she told me, I knew she’d identified one of my greatest weaknesses as a parent. I always want my son to be having a good time, and there’s some part of me that worries if I’m not actively trying to make his time better, it’s not as good as it could be.

According to recent reports, as a baby, if he was enjoying gnawing on a particular teether, I’d jump in to give him another one, too. Oh, he likes the dog at this park? Let’s leave this park with one dog to find a dog park full of dogs. If he were having a perfectly nice time throwing rocks in a puddle, I’d offer to find him better rocks that would make an even bigger splash.

There’s an impulse in us as parents not just to nurture, to make sure all gaps are closed. We want to provide the complete package for our kids, to make sure all their needs are met in the best possible way. And that urge is good. It’s why we don’t abandon them in the woods when they won’t stop crying at 4 a.m. and why we keep feeding them every day even when they throw everything we offer on the floor. But it also means we can fail to notice when we aren’t needed.

Industry observers note that what “don’t make a happy kid happier” does is remind me that sometimes, just being happy is enough. Kids live in a world of the immediate now, where whatever they are doing is often the only thing on their minds. Yes, there might be bigger, splashier rocks to throw in the puddle, but the rocks they have in their hand suit them just fine. What I think I’m doing when I do this is helping my son, but what I’m actually doing is pointing out that what he’s doing might not be good enough. Suddenly he can see that the emperor has no clothes, and it actually becomes not good enough.

Industry observers note that we never did find the cat. But I paid the price for my misstep in toddler currency: a temper tantrum. He settled down eventually, and by the time we left the farm, he was happily kicking and chatting in his stroller. I thought about stopping for ice cream at the gift shop, but I decided against it this time. He was just fine.

#44774. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

📅 03 Jan 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2905 w)
